Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $42/unit; runway is 9 months. Red lines: no public per-model test failure rates, and no retrofit shut-off deadline under 6 years. CEO wants S2 kept loose because Hearth 10 exceeds the proposed 5% limit.

For evidence-based drafting, please share relevant incident, thermal-test, retrofit-capability, and suppression-cost figures for your fleet/models. We should distinguish regulator/customer reporting from public disclosure of per-model test rates.

Halcyon figures: fleet-wide thermal incidents were 8.1 per 100,000 installed units last year, with 4 incidents not reported to a regulator. For our flagship, the 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate is 3.9%, while its thermal incident rate was 9.9 per 100,000 installed units last year. 81% of our installed units support remote emergency shut-off. Built-in suppression would cost about $67 per unit. We support distinguishing regulator/customer reporting from broader public disclosure, but per-model test results should be available to customers buying that model.

HC-1 requires test results not be kept confidential from model customers; HC-2 bars suppression deadlines sooner than 36 months after adoption.

That keeps Hearth 10 within the limit while preserving meaningful testing. I’ll also draft prompt regulator/customer incident reporting and a model-specific recall trigger.

Manufacturers must report each thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 48 hours when the incident presents a potential safety risk to their unit or requires customer action. Reports must include the known circumstances, model and unit identification where available, and any immediate safety instructions. These reporting duties do not require public disclosure of individual-company or per-model test failure rates.

These results are not required to be published to the general public. Manufacturers must retain supporting test records and provide them to regulators on request.
